tracks.name: Components & JSX
tracks.description: Build UI out of small functions: write your first component, embed expressions in JSX, compose nested components, and render conditionally and in lists.

lessons.title: 1. Write your first component
lessons.summary: Build UI out of small JavaScript functions that return JSX.

activities.title: Read a component definition
activities.instruction: A function component returns JSX. Calling render() mounts it, and screen lets you read back what was rendered.

activities.title: Predict the output
activities.question: What must a function return to count as a React component?
activities.explanation: A component's job is to describe UI as JSX; React turns that description into real DOM elements.

activities.title: Greet the class
activities.instruction: Create a component named Greeting that renders an <h1> saying 'Hello, React', then render and log its text.

activities.title: Recall function component syntax
activities.instruction: Write a component that renders an <h1> and print its exact text.
activities.starterCode:
// Define a component that renders

Welcome to React
hints: Capitalize the component's name so React treats it as a component, not an HTML tag.

teaching.text: A React component is just a function whose name starts with a capital letter and that returns JSX — a description of what should appear on the screen. This course renders components with `render()` and reads the result back with `screen`, the same helpers real React tests use.
JSX looks like HTML but compiles to plain JavaScript function calls, so it can only appear where an expression is allowed.

lessons.task: Write a component that renders an <h1> and print its exact text.
lessons.starterCode:
// Define a component that renders

Welcome to React
hints: Capitalize the component's name so React treats it as a component, not an HTML tag.

lessons.title: 2. Embed expressions in JSX
lessons.summary: Drop any JavaScript expression into JSX with curly braces.

activities.title: Read an embedded expression
activities.instruction: The value inside the curly braces is evaluated and inserted into the rendered text.

activities.title: Predict the output
activities.question: What can you put inside { } in JSX?
activities.explanation: Curly braces accept any expression, including variables, function calls, and arithmetic.

activities.title: Show a computed score
activities.instruction: Store 2 and 3 in variables, add them inside JSX, and print the total.

activities.title: Recall JSX expressions
activities.instruction: Embed a computed value in JSX and print it exactly.
activities.starterCode:
// Render

Score: {value}

where value is computed from 80 + 7
hints: Wrap the arithmetic in curly braces inside the JSX.

teaching.text: Curly braces switch JSX back into JavaScript mode. Anything that evaluates to a value — a variable, a function call, arithmetic — can go inside them.
You can't embed statements like if or for directly in JSX; use expressions such as the ternary operator instead.

lessons.task: Embed a computed value in JSX and print it exactly.
lessons.starterCode:
// Render

Score: {value}

where value is computed from 80 + 7
hints: Wrap the arithmetic in curly braces inside the JSX.

lessons.title: 3. Compose components with children
lessons.summary: Nest components inside each other and pass content through children.

activities.title: Read a children prop
activities.instruction: Card doesn't know what's inside it — it just renders whatever children it receives.

activities.title: Predict the output
activities.question: How does a component access the content placed between its tags?
activities.explanation: React automatically passes nested JSX to a component as props.children.

activities.title: Nest a Panel
activities.instruction: Create a Panel component that renders its children, then nest a heading named 'Settings' inside it.

activities.title: Recall composition with children
activities.instruction: Build a wrapper component and render nested text through it.
activities.starterCode:
// Render

Panel: Settings

through a wrapping component's children
hints: Render {children} inside the wrapper component's JSX.

teaching.text: Whatever you put between a component's opening and closing tags is passed to it as the special `children` prop, letting components wrap other components.
Composition with children is how React builds layout pieces like cards, panels, and modals.

lessons.task: Build a wrapper component and render nested text through it.
lessons.starterCode:
// Render

Panel: Settings

through a wrapping component's children
hints: Render {children} inside the wrapper component's JSX.

lessons.title: 4. Conditionally render UI
lessons.summary: Choose what to render with ternaries and logical operators.

activities.title: Read a conditional render
activities.instruction: The ternary picks one of two strings to render based on the isOnline prop.

activities.title: Predict the output
activities.question: Which operator lets you pick between two JSX outputs based on a condition?
activities.explanation: The ternary operator evaluates to one of two expressions, which is exactly what JSX needs.

activities.title: Flip the status
activities.instruction: Render Status with isOnline set to false and print the resulting text.

activities.title: Recall conditional rendering
activities.instruction: Render a component whose text depends on a boolean prop.
activities.starterCode:
// Render

{isOnline ? 'Online' : 'Offline'}

with isOnline=false
hints: Pass isOnline={false} to the component.

teaching.text: Since JSX is just an expression, ordinary JavaScript operators like the ternary (`? :`) and `&&` are enough to decide what gets rendered.
Use `value && <Component />` to render something only when value is truthy, and nothing otherwise.

lessons.task: Render a component whose text depends on a boolean prop.
lessons.starterCode:
// Render

{isOnline ? 'Online' : 'Offline'}

with isOnline=false
hints: Pass isOnline={false} to the component.

lessons.title: 5. Render lists with keys
lessons.summary: Turn arrays into elements with map, and give each one a stable key.

activities.title: Read a rendered list
activities.instruction: map produces one <li> per array item, and key helps React match items between renders.

activities.title: Predict the output
activities.question: Why does each item in a rendered list need a unique key?
choices: So React can track which item is which across renders
So the browser can sort the list alphabetically
Keys are only needed for styling
activities.answer: So React can track which item is which across renders
activities.explanation: React uses the key to match list items between renders instead of re-creating every element.

activities.title: Render numbers
activities.instruction: Render a list of the numbers 1, 2, and 3 and print them joined by commas.

activities.title: Recall list rendering
activities.instruction: Map an array to list items and print their joined text.
activities.starterCode: // Render <li> elements for [1, 2, 3] and log their joined text
hints: Give each <li> a key based on the item's value.

teaching.text: Array.prototype.map turns data into JSX elements. Each element in a list needs a `key` prop so React can track which item is which across re-renders.
Prefer a stable, unique id for `key` over the array index, especially if the list can be reordered.

lessons.task: Map an array to list items and print their joined text.
lessons.starterCode: // Render <li> elements for [1, 2, 3] and log their joined text
hints: Give each <li> a key based on the item's value.

tracks.name: Props & Data Flow
tracks.description: Pass data into components with props, set default values, forward callbacks, spread props through wrappers, and model UI variants from a single status prop.

lessons.title: 1. Pass data with props
lessons.summary: Send data into a component through named props, just like function arguments.

activities.title: Read a prop
activities.instruction: The name attribute on <Greeting /> becomes the name prop inside the function.

activities.title: Predict the output
activities.question: How does a parent send data to a child component?
choices: By passing props as JSX attributes
By editing the child's source file
activities.answer: By passing props as JSX attributes
activities.explanation: JSX attributes become the props object the child component receives as its argument.

activities.title: Greet someone else
activities.instruction: Render Greeting with name set to 'Noah' and print the greeting.

activities.title: Recall passing props
activities.instruction: Pass a prop into a component and print the rendered text.
activities.starterCode: // Render <Greeting name='Noah' /> and log its text
hints: Read the prop with destructuring: function Greeting({ name }).

teaching.text: Props are the arguments you pass to a component when you use it: `<Greeting name="Maya" />` gives Greeting a `name` prop of "Maya".
Props flow in one direction, from parent to child, and a component should never modify the props it receives.

lessons.task: Pass a prop into a component and print the rendered text.
lessons.starterCode: // Render <Greeting name='Noah' /> and log its text
hints: Read the prop with destructuring: function Greeting({ name }).

lessons.title: 2. Set default prop values
lessons.summary: Give a prop a fallback value for when the caller doesn't provide one.

activities.title: Read a default prop
activities.instruction: No name prop is passed here, so the default value is used instead.

activities.title: Predict the output
activities.question: When does a destructured default value get used?
choices: Every time, regardless of the prop
Only when the prop is an empty string
activities.explanation: Default values in destructuring only kick in for undefined, not for other falsy values.

activities.title: Override the default
activities.instruction: Render Greeting again, this time passing name='Priya', and print the result.

activities.title: Recall default prop values
activities.instruction: Give a prop a default and render the component without passing that prop.
activities.starterCode: // Render <Badge /> with a role prop that defaults to 'guest'
hints: Write the default inside the destructuring pattern: { role = 'guest' }.

teaching.text: Destructuring supports default values directly: `{ name = "friend" }` falls back to "friend" whenever the caller omits the name prop.
Defaults only apply when a prop is undefined, not when it's an empty string or 0.

lessons.task: Give a prop a default and render the component without passing that prop.
lessons.starterCode: // Render <Badge /> with a role prop that defaults to 'guest'
hints: Write the default inside the destructuring pattern: { role = 'guest' }.

lessons.title: 3. Pass functions as props
lessons.summary: Let a child notify its parent of events by calling a function passed in as a prop.

activities.title: Read a callback prop
activities.instruction: Clicking the button calls the onPress prop, which runs the parent's handlePress function.

activities.title: Predict the output
activities.question: How does a child component inform its parent that something happened?
choices: By calling a callback function passed in as a prop
By directly modifying the parent's state
It can't; only parents can talk to children
activities.answer: By calling a callback function passed in as a prop
activities.explanation: Passing a function as a prop lets the child invoke parent logic without knowing what that logic does.

activities.title: Log a different message
activities.instruction: Change handlePress to log 'Saved!' instead, then click the button and print the log.

activities.title: Recall callback props
activities.instruction: Pass a callback into a button component and trigger it with a click.
activities.starterCode: // Pass an onPress callback to a Button that logs 'Deleted!' when clicked
hints: Attach the callback prop to the button's onClick handler.

teaching.text: Functions are ordinary values in JavaScript, so a parent can pass a callback down as a prop. The child calls it in response to an event, letting the parent react without the child knowing any details.
Callback props are how React "talks back up" the component tree — data flows down, events flow up through callbacks.

lessons.task: Pass a callback into a button component and trigger it with a click.
lessons.starterCode: // Pass an onPress callback to a Button that logs 'Deleted!' when clicked
hints: Attach the callback prop to the button's onClick handler.

lessons.title: 4. Destructure and spread props
lessons.summary: Pull specific props out with destructuring, or forward a whole props object with spread.

activities.title: Read spread props
activities.instruction: ProfilePic forwards every prop it receives straight through to Avatar using {...props}.

activities.title: Predict the output
activities.question: What does {...props} do when passed to a JSX element?
choices: It spreads every key of props onto that element as individual props
It renders the props object as visible text
It deletes all props from the element
activities.answer: It spreads every key of props onto that element as individual props
activities.explanation: Spread syntax expands an object's own properties into individual props on the element.

activities.title: Forward a title prop
activities.instruction: Add a title prop to Avatar, forward it through ProfilePic, and read it back with getByTitle.

activities.title: Recall spreading props
activities.instruction: Forward props through a wrapper component and read an attribute from the result.
activities.starterCode: // Forward src and alt props through a wrapper to an
hints: Use {...props} on the inner element inside the wrapper component.

teaching.text: Destructuring props keeps a component's signature self-documenting. The spread operator does the reverse — it forwards every prop on an object to another component in one step.
Spreading props is convenient for thin wrapper components, but can hide exactly which props a component actually uses.

lessons.task: Forward props through a wrapper component and read an attribute from the result.
lessons.starterCode: // Forward src and alt props through a wrapper to an
hints: Use {...props} on the inner element inside the wrapper component.

lessons.title: 5. Render UI variants from a status prop
lessons.summary: Use a single prop to switch between the loading, error, and ready states of a UI.

activities.title: Read a status-driven render
activities.instruction: Status checks the state prop and returns different JSX for each case.

activities.title: Predict the output
activities.question: What does Status render when state is 'loading'?
activities.explanation: The first matching branch, state === 'loading', returns the loading text.

activities.title: Render the error state
activities.instruction: Render Status with state set to 'error' and print the resulting text.

activities.title: Recall variant rendering
activities.instruction: Render a component whose output depends on a status prop, using the default branch.
activities.starterCode: // Render <Status state='ready' /> and fall through to the default branch
hints: Pass a state value that matches neither 'loading' nor 'error'.

teaching.text: Real screens usually have more than one shape: loading, error, and success are the classic trio. A single "state" prop with early returns keeps each case easy to read.
This pattern scales naturally into useState later in the course, where the state prop becomes state you manage yourself.

lessons.task: Render a component whose output depends on a status prop, using the default branch.
lessons.starterCode: // Render <Status state='ready' /> and fall through to the default branch
hints: Pass a state value that matches neither 'loading' nor 'error'.

Price never re-renders here because its amount prop stays 20, even though App re-renders on every click.

teaching.text: Without useCallback, a component creates a brand-new function on every render, which breaks React.memo on any child it's passed to. useCallback returns the same function reference as long as its dependencies don't change.
useCallback is most valuable when the callback is passed to a memoized child or another hook's dependency array.

teaching.text: A custom hook is just a function that calls other hooks. Naming it useSomething lets React enforce the rules of hooks and lets you reuse the same stateful logic across components.
Custom hooks share logic, not state — each component that calls useCounter gets its own independent count.

teaching.text: Combine everything from this course into one small, real app: a reducer drives state transitions, event handlers dispatch actions, and derived values like the remaining count are computed straight from state on every render.
This is the same shape as most real React features: state describes the truth, and the UI is just a function of it.
